title: Seven Years After My First Love Disappeared, Four Little Girls Walked Into My Life—And Their Mother Revealed the Secret My Family Had Buried

blocks.text: My name is Alexander Whitmore, and until that evening, I believed my life was carefully arranged.
I was thirty-four, the only son of a wealthy family, and the expected successor to my grandfather’s investment empire.
My parents had planned almost every important decision in my life.
My education. My career. My friendships.
Her name was Margot Ashford. She came from another influential family, and our engagement was supposed to unite two powerful business dynasties.
But I had learned that love wasn’t something my family considered necessary.
Seven years earlier, I had loved someone with everything I had.
She wasn’t wealthy. Her father had owned a small neighborhood bookstore, and she worked as an illustrator for children’s books.
She laughed loudly, hated expensive restaurants, and believed that the best mornings began with coffee and long conversations.
She was standing in front of one of her illustrations, arguing with a visitor who claimed children’s books didn’t need meaningful stories.
I had never seen anyone defend something so passionately.
Three months later, I was completely in love.
For the first time, I wanted something that had nothing to do with my family’s expectations.
I wanted a small house, a garden, children, and a woman who would laugh at my terrible cooking.
One morning, I received a short message.
Alexander, I’m sorry. I can’t continue this relationship. Please don’t look for me.
I visited her apartment, but someone else was living there.
My mother told me Elena had been seeing another man.
My father said she had only been interested in our money.
My grandfather advised me to forget her before she damaged the family’s reputation.
Until my mother showed me what she claimed was proof.
A photograph of Elena standing beside another man, holding his arm outside a hotel.
Seven years later, I was standing in a luxury restaurant preparing for the biggest engagement announcement of my life.
Margot was beautiful, intelligent, and perfectly suited to my family’s world.
My father considered her an excellent investment.
And I was expected to put a diamond ring on her finger that evening.
At around six thirty, I excused myself to visit the restroom.
They were standing near the sinks, wearing identical navy-blue dresses with little white ribbons.
One was trying to dry her hands while another complained that the hand dryer was too loud.
The fourth was carefully fixing her sister’s hair.
Then one girl tilted her head and pushed her brown hair behind her ear.
Elena used to do it whenever she was concentrating.
They looked so much alike that I wondered whether they were quadruplets.
Then a woman’s voice came from behind them.
“Girls! I’ve been looking everywhere for you!”
She looked older, naturally. There were faint lines near her eyes, and her hair was slightly shorter.
But she was unmistakably the woman I had loved.
For several seconds, neither of us spoke.
Finally, I managed to say, “You’re alive.”
“Nothing. I just… I thought I’d never see you again.”
She glanced at my suit, then noticed the diamond ring box in my hand.
“Seven years ago, I was pregnant. When I called you, your mother answered. She told me you knew about the pregnancy and wanted nothing to do with me.”
I felt something cold spread through my chest.
“She said you were engaged to someone else. She told me not to embarrass your family by demanding money or attention.”
“Neither did I know you were looking for me.”
We stood there, separated by seven years of lies.
Then one of the girls tugged at Elena’s dress.
“Yes,” I whispered. “If you’ll let me be.”
Then the smallest one stepped forward and held out a little hand.
She gave me an address and told me she would wait for me after the girls had dinner.
Then she took their hands and walked away.
I remained in the restroom long after they disappeared.
The engagement announcement was approaching.
But for the first time in seven years, I knew exactly what I wanted.
I returned to the conservatory at seven thirty.
“Where have you been? Margot is getting nervous.”
For a moment, I thought I saw fear in her eyes.
“Did you tell her I wanted nothing to do with her?”
